- If sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.2) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- If sentiment is negative (≤0.0) or neutral, model often underestimates; adjust downward bias, especially if recent price is rising.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >10% from prior day), model frequently overshoots and fails to correct; apply a “cool-down” rule: reduce forecast by 5–10% for next 3–5 days post-spike.
- When sentiment is high and price is trending up, model often fails to capture mean reversion; add a “reversion buffer” — if forecast exceeds 20% above recent 10-day average, reduce by 10–15%.
- If model forecast is flat or rising slowly but true price shows strong upward momentum, sentiment is often positive — model underestimates; increase forecast by 2–5% for next 3–5 days if sentiment >0.2.
- If sentiment is low and price is falling, model often overcorrects downward — forecast should be slightly above true price to avoid “double-dip” errors.
- For 30-day horizon, model tends to overfit recent trends; apply a “smoothing filter” — average last 5–7 days’ price + sentiment to adjust forecast baseline.
